**Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements**
```{r}
score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}

score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}

scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}
```

*Question 4*

  Since 10 is greater than 5, R executes the first condition and stop checking the remaining conditions.
  
```{r}
 x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print ("B")
} else {
  print("C")
} 
```

*Question 6f: Applying Conditional Statements*

```{r}

```
*Question 6f.1*
             
```{r}
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 
  0.30 * grades$Midterm +
  0.40 * grades$Final

print(grades[,c("Name", "FinalGrade")])
```
*Question 6f.2*

```{r}
grades$Result <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >=75, "Passed", "Failed")
)

print(grades[,c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Result")])
```
*Question 6f.3*
  
```{r, eval=TRUE}
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair",
         "Needs Improvement"))))
)

print(grades[,c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Remarks")])
```
*Question 6f.4*
  
```{r}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(
  grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK"
)

print(grades[,c("Name", "Attendance", "AttendanceFlag")])
```
*Question 6f.5*

```{r}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(
  !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) &
  grades$FinalGrade >= 90 &
  grades$Attendance >= 90,
  "Yes", "No"
)
grades$Honors
```
*Question 6f.6*
  
```{r}
grades$Result <- ""

for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    grades$Result[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    grades$Result[i] <- "Passed"
  } else {
    grades$Result[i] <- "Failed"
  }
}

print(grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Result")])
```
*Question 6f.7*

   R gives a warning because the if statement expects only one TRUE or FALSE value, but grades$FinalGrade contains multiple values. The loop version avoids this problem by checking each student's FinalGrade one at time.

**Part D: Exporting Results to .csv**
```{r}

```
*Question 7*

a) The full processed grades table was successfully exported.
b) I used row.names = FALSE to avoid adding an extra row number column.
c) I selected only the required columns and exported qualified students to honors_list.csv using row.names = FALSE.
d) The exported CSV file were read back into R to verify.
  
```{r}
write.csv(grades, 
          "students_grades_processed.csv", 
          row.names = FALSE)

at_risk_students <- grades[
  grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk_students) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk_students,
            "at_risk_students.csv",
            row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No at-risk students found")
}

at_risk_students

honors_list <- grades[
  grades$Honors == "Yes",
  c("StudentID", "Name", "Section",
    "FinalGrade", "Attendance")
]

if (nrow(honors_list) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors_list,
            "honors_list.csv",
            row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  print("No honors candidates found")
}

honors_list

processed <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv")
at_risk <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv")
honors <- read.csv("honors_list.csv")

print("Processed Grades:")
print(head(processed))

print("At-Risk Students:")
print(head(at_risk))

print("Honors List:")
print(head(honors))
```
*Question 8*

1. The missing midterm appears as NA in the exported csv file because the value is missing.
2. Without row.names = FALSE, R automatically adds an extra column containing row numbers. This create unnecessary column in the file.

```{r}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
         ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial", "None"))
)
grades$Scholarship

scholarship_candidates <- grades[
  grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"), ]

print(scholarship_candidates)

if (nrow(scholarship_candidates) > 0) {
  write.csv(scholarship_candidates,
            "scholarship_candidates.csv",
            row.names = FALSE)
  print("Scholarship candidates exported successfully")
} else {
  print("No scholarship candidates found")
}

table(grades$Scholarship)
```
*Question 9*

a) Students with missing final grades are marked Pending, those with a grade of 95 or higher and attendance of 90% or higher receive Full, those with a grade of 85 or higher and attendance of 90% or higher receive Partial, and everyone else receives None.
b) The code above already use nested ifelse() statements. It checks missing grades first, then full, partial and assigns none to everyone else.
c) I selected the students who qualified for either Full or Partial scholarships using the %in% operator. Only students with these two scholarship categories are included in the scholarship_candidates data frame.
d) The scholarship candidates were exported to scholarship_candidates.csv using row.names = FALSE to avoid adding an extra row-number column.
e) The output: Full = 1,  None = 9, Partial = 4, Pending = 1

```{r}

```
*Question 10*

1. I checked is.na() first because missing values cannot be compared properly with numbers. This prevents incorrect results.
2. Students with missing grades might not be properly classified
as Incomplete because the Failed condition is checked first.
3. ifelse() is better when working with an entire vector or column
because it checks every element. if ... else is better when checking one value or making decisions inside a loop.
4. Reading an exported CSV back into R helps verify that the file was saved correctly and that the data and columns are complete.
